segments.title: Type 26 as a submarine hunter
segments.body: The Type 26 is designed to find and destroy submarines. The submariners' joke divides vessels into submarines and targets, but a submarine that can approach unseen is still vulnerable to a ship equipped to hunt it. Losing the ship and surviving the sinking are separate risks. The historical comparison gives the surface crew a better chance of survival.

evidence.note: Submariners' joke about surface ships as targets, the vulnerability of submarines and the relative chances of crew survival after a sinking.

segments.summary: A submariners' joke about surface ships as targets introduces the threat the Type 26 was built to counter.

segments.title: Why a specialist ASW frigate costs so much
segments.body: The comparison starts with an illustrative cost of roughly £1 billion for a nuclear submarine. If an escort is expected to face an opponent of that calibre, there is little reason to assume it will come much cheaper. The frigate also protects the rest of the task group. The stakes include the troops and supplies headed for a combat zone and any air power the group is carrying.

evidence.note: Recurring question about escort cost, answered by comparing the capability needed to face a nuclear submarine with the value of the force under escort. The £1 billion figure is illustrative.

segments.summary: A rough nuclear submarine cost illustrates why a frigate built to face one is expensive and what that expenditure protects.
segments.question: Why is a specialist anti-submarine frigate such as the Type 26 so expensive?
segments.answerShort: A high-end escort has to be able to hunt a capable nuclear submarine while protecting the troops, supplies or air power the task group carries.

segments.title: How to recognise a purpose-built ASW frigate
segments.body: Raft-mounted machinery and hull shaping are two ways to recognise the Type 26's priorities. Both show that submarine hunting affects the ship's basic design. The design draws on roughly a century or more of anti-submarine warfare practice. Exercises and combat helped show which methods were worth incorporating.

evidence.note: Machinery rafting and hull shaping as signs of ASW specialisation, with exercises and combat informing the design over roughly a century or more.

segments.summary: Raft-mounted machinery and hull shaping show how more than a century of submarine-hunting experience informed the Type 26.
segments.question: What shows that the Type 26 is designed around anti-submarine warfare?
segments.answerShort: Raft-mounted machinery and hull shaping apply lessons from anti-submarine exercises and combat.

segments.title: Self-defence on an ASW specialist
segments.body: Submarine hunting sets the Type 26's design priority. The ship still needs to defend itself against air attack. It also has to earn its place when no submarine threat is present by supporting other operations. Those demands limit how far the design can specialise.

evidence.note: Air self-defence and support for other operations are requirements even for a dedicated submarine hunter.

segments.summary: Submarine hunting sets the design priority, while air self-defence and other operations still make demands on the ship.

segments.title: River and Hunter class roles
segments.body: The Canadian River and Australian Hunter classes both start from a ship designed to hunt submarines. In the Canadian case, the range of other capabilities helps explain the choice of the destroyer designation. Whether that designation is the best fit is open to debate. Both variants retain submarine hunting as a central job.

evidence.note: Shared ASW foundation of the River and Hunter classes, and the case for Canada's destroyer designation based on the River class's broader capabilities.

segments.summary: The River and Hunter classes share a submarine-hunting design. Canada's destroyer label reflects the range of capabilities planned for the River class.

segments.title: Directing a task group's submarine hunt
segments.body: The lead ASW ship needs to keep track of the submarine hunt across the task group. That picture lets it direct the search as well as take part in it. The analogy is an air-defence destroyer or, in a US group, possibly a cruiser. Uncrewed assets can supplement the frigate's existing ASW capability.

evidence.note: Lead ASW coordination, the analogy with air-defence command and uncrewed support. The specific support function is unclear at 3:36.

segments.summary: The Type 26 is designed to lead a task group's submarine hunt, in much the same way an air-defence ship directs that part of the group's defence.

segments.title: City-class frigates in a British carrier group
segments.body: The Royal Navy's City class is designed to operate in carrier groups. Carrier aircraft and other escorts provide longer-range air defence. The frigate still needs to defend itself against a range of threats, but it can put more of its effort into finding submarines. The force can cover several threats at once by combining ships with different specialties.

evidence.note: Division of labour between the City class's self-defence and submarine hunting and the longer-range air defence provided by carrier aircraft and other ships.

segments.summary: Carrier aircraft and other escorts handle longer-range air defence, giving the City class room to concentrate on submarine hunting.

segments.title: Canada's River-class plans and allied orders
segments.body: Canada is expected to use its River-class ships mainly in allied task groups. A Canadian surface action group is a less likely possibility. One projection puts the Canadian order above the City and Hunter orders combined. It may still be larger if the Norwegian order is included, depending on how Britain allocates build slots to Norway and settles its own order.

evidence.note: Service in allied task groups as the expected Canadian role, with a Canadian surface action group a less likely possibility.
Tentative comparison of orders without specific totals, subject to UK build-slot allocation and the final British order.

segments.summary: The River class is expected mainly to work in allied formations. Canada's planned order is compared with British, Australian and Norwegian orders.

segments.title: How River and Hunter could reinforce a British group
segments.body: A River or Hunter in a British task group could serve two parts of the screen. A City-class frigate would lead the submarine hunt, with the allied escort reinforcing it. The same escort could also support the Type 45 Daring class or its successor in air defence. The example shows why the allied variant needs to be able to supplement more than one specialist.

evidence.note: Hypothetical support by a River or Hunter for both the City class's submarine hunt and the Type 45's air defence.

segments.summary: In a British task group, a River or Hunter could support the City class's submarine hunt and help the Type 45 Daring class with air defence.

segments.title: Why announced Royal Navy plans can change
segments.body: Announcing a Type 45 successor leaves open what Britain will eventually build. An unnamed amphibious ship programme provides the example. Britain reportedly left twice, proposed pursuing a different solution each time and returned on both occasions. Even an announced change of direction can give way to a return to an earlier plan.

evidence.note: Caution about Type 45 successor announcements, illustrated by the account of two British departures from and returns to an unnamed amphibious ship programme.

segments.summary: An unnamed amphibious ship programme that Britain reportedly left and rejoined twice illustrates the uncertainty around the Type 45's eventual successor.

segments.title: River and Hunter in US or Japanese task groups
segments.body: The River and Hunter variants could work in American or Japanese task groups as well as British ones. Which nation supplies the core ships changes the formation the escort has to fit into. Carriers and amphibious ships are common examples of core ships. Their large command facilities give the group a place from which to direct operations.

evidence.note: Possible US and Japanese partners and the command facilities that make carriers or amphibious ships suitable as a task group's core.

segments.summary: A River or Hunter could join a US or Japanese formation. The escort would have to adapt to a group organised around another navy's command ship.

segments.title: How NATO groups can reinforce a carrier screen
segments.body: Standing maritime patrols and surface action groups can operate under an escort's lead. In the Atlantic or Mediterranean, they can join a carrier battle group and add ships to its screen. One explanation for this reinforcement role is that spending cuts left carrier groups with fewer escorts of their own. In that view, expecting future conflicts to be wars of choice was a weak justification for the cuts.

evidence.note: Standing maritime groups as potential reinforcements for carrier screens. The link to budget cuts and the expectation of wars of choice is an interpretation.

segments.summary: Standing NATO maritime patrols and surface action groups can add escorts to a carrier force in the Atlantic or Mediterranean.

segments.title: Type 26 deck layout and ASW mission spaces
segments.body: Hull shape and the provision for handling sensor data are part of the Type 26's ASW design. A walk through the deck layout starts at the planned 5-inch gun forward and picks out several missile positions. The large flight deck aft and the hangar give aviation substantial space. The multi-mission bay can take uncrewed systems to assist the submarine hunt, with scope for other systems as well.

evidence.note: Forward 5-inch gun and several missile spaces, followed by the aft flight deck, hangar and multi-mission bay. Exact missile locations depend on the visuals.

segments.summary: The forward gun and missile spaces orient the deck walkthrough before it turns to the space set aside for aircraft and uncrewed systems.

segments.title: Shipboard torpedo launchers and the close-range problem
segments.body: A shipboard torpedo launcher would be a conventional fit on a submarine hunter. It can often fire the same torpedoes the embarked helicopter carries. It gives the ship a close-range fallback, though a submarine that close may already be able to fire back. Even with that limitation, the launcher is a feature one would expect to find on an ASW escort.

evidence.note: Apparent omission of a shipboard launcher in the fit under review. A typical launcher fires the helicopter's torpedo and gives the escort a close-range response.

segments.summary: A shipboard launcher would give the frigate a close-range way to fire torpedoes. The Type 26 fit under review appears to omit it.

segments.title: Type 2150 bow sonar and the Type 2087 towed array
segments.body: The bow is shaped to keep the water flowing cleanly past the Ultra Electronics Type 2150 hull-mounted sonar. The Type 2087 towed array is expected to see more use in the hunt. Other units can coordinate with the frigate and bring their own towed arrays into the search. The frigate can draw on several sensors without depending on any single system.

evidence.note: Bow shaping for clean flow past the Type 2150, greater expected use of the Type 2087 and coordination with other units' towed arrays.

segments.summary: Bow shaping keeps the flow past the hull-mounted sonar clean, while the Type 2087 towed array is expected to see more use.

segments.title: Computing, cooling and propulsion for submarine hunting
segments.body: The Type 26 needs to make use of sensor data from several ASW assets. That requires space for computers and a layout that lets the ship cool them. Supplying power is part of the same design problem. A gas turbine, diesel engines and electric motors figure in the machinery fit.

evidence.note: Multiple sources of ASW data, computer space and cooling, and provision for power. The exact propulsion arrangement is unclear at 9:43 to 9:51.

segments.summary: Collecting data from several ASW assets makes computer space, cooling and power part of the Type 26's design problem.

segments.title: Why a quieter frigate hears submarines farther away
segments.body: Machinery is raft-mounted and positioned to keep the frigate quiet. Noise from the ship itself can mask the sounds its sensors are trying to pick up. Reducing that interference improves the prospects of hearing a submarine farther away. It also makes the frigate harder for the submarine to hear, though the priority in this explanation is the frigate's own detection performance.

evidence.note: Machinery rafting and placement reduce the noise that can mask a submarine on the frigate's own sensors. Reduced audibility to the submarine is a secondary benefit.

segments.summary: Rafting and machinery placement reduce the ship's own noise so its sonar can pick up submarines at greater distance.
